Fully discrete scheme for the fifth-order KdV-Burgers-Fisher equation using Strang splitting and Fourier collocation methods

Nurcan Gücüyenen Kaymak Affiliation: Department of Management Information Systems, Faculty of Economics, Administrative and Social Sciences,
Dogus University, Istanbul, 34480, Turkey    Fatma Zürnacı-Yetiş Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Engineering, Istanbul Technical University, Maslak, Istanbul, 34469, Turkey    Muaz Seydaoğlu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Art and Science, Muş Alparslan University, Muş, 49250, Turkey
Abstract

Operator splitting is an effective technique for the numerical solution of nonlinear partial differential equations by decomposing a complex problem into simpler subproblems. In this study, we present and analyze a fully discrete scheme for the fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers-Fisher equation (KBF) by combining Strang splitting for time discretization with the Fourier collocation method for spatial discretization. In particular, the Fourier collocation method is an essential component of the proposed fully discrete scheme and yields spectral accuracy in space under suitable regularity assumptions. The KBF equation describes the interaction of reaction, dissipative, and dispersive mechanisms by incorporating the Fisher reaction term together with Burgers-type diffusion and higher-order KdV dispersion. The equation is split into a linear operator and a nonlinear operator, and the resulting subproblems are solved within the Strang splitting framework. Convergence is analyzed in the Sobolev space HsH^{s}. The local error is derived using operator-theoretic arguments in Banach spaces together with Lie commutator estimates, while the global error is obtained using the Lady Windermere’s fan argument. The analysis yields second-order convergence in time and spectral convergence in space. Numerical results confirm the theoretical error estimates and demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed fully discrete scheme.

Keywords: 
Nonlinear PDE Operator splitting method Fourier collocation methodConvergence analysis.

1 Introduction

The study of nonlinear dispersive wave phenomena occupies a central role in the theory of partial differential equations (PDE), as many large-scale and complex physical processes are described and analyzed through PDE models. The investigation of both exact and numerical solutions of nonlinear partial differential equations constitutes a significant area of research in mathematical science. Over the years, numerous studies have been conducted by researchers on wave equations. In [2], the fifth-order nonlinear fractional Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equations are analyzed using the ρ\rho-homotopy perturbation method. In [5], the generalized Burgers-Fisher equation is studied by the meshfree spectral method. The KdV-Kawahara equation is analyzed using trigonometric quintic B-spline basis collocation method in [6]. Time fractional nonlinear Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers equation arising in shallow water waves is examined with the help of the finite element method combined quintic B-spline in [7]. In [3, 4], numerical solutions of the BBM-Burger equations are studied using the collocation method with the quintic Hermit spline and the quartic B-spline. Moreover, the fifth-order KdV-Burgers-Fisher equation is studied using the finite-element method combined quintic B-spline technique in [8]. In [9], the unified F-expansion method is considered for the soliton solutions of the fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries equation. In [1], the numerical solution to the fifth-order KdV-type equations is discussed with the help of the Legendre collocation technique.

In this study, we focus on the numerical solution of the fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers-Fisher equation (KBF) using the Strang splitting method. This equation serves as a representative example of dispersion-dissipation-reaction type systems given as follows:

yt=ν​yx​x−μ​yx​x​x+γ​yx​x​x​x​x−ε​y2​yx+ϵ​y​(1−y),y⁡(t0)=y0,y_{t}=\nu y_{xx}-\mu y_{xxx}+\gamma y_{xxxxx}-\varepsilon y^{2}\,y_{x}+\epsilon y\bigl(1-y\bigr),\,\,y(t_{0})=y_{0},\ \ (1)

where x∈(a,b)x\in(a,b), t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. This equation incorporates the reaction mechanism of the Fisher model together with the dispersive effects of the KdV equation and the dissipative behavior associated with the Burgers equation. When μ=γ=0\mu=\gamma=0 and the nonlinear convective term is neglected, the above equation (1) reduces to the classical Fisher equation. When ν=ϵ=0\nu=\epsilon=0, equation (1) corresponds to a modified fifth-order KdV-type equation. For μ=ϵ=0\mu=\epsilon=0, equation (1) corresponds to a modified Kawahara-type equation, and for γ=ϵ=0\gamma=\epsilon=0, equation (1) reduces to a modified KdV–Burgers-type equation.

The operator splitting method is a practical and efficient approach to obtain numerical solutions to nonlinear partial differential equations. The idea behind splitting methods is to decompose a complicated problem into a set of simple subproblems, then each equation can be studied separately with an appropriate method, see [10, 11]. In [12], the Strang splitting method is applied to the evolutionary Schrödinger equation over long times. In [13, 14, 16], Benjamin-Bona-Mahony type equations are analyzed with time splitting errors using Strang and Lie-Trotter splitting methods. The analysis of nonlinear convection diffusion equations is examined using the Strang splitting combined compact difference method in [15]. In [18], the Lie-Trotter and Strang splitting methods are applied to the dispersive-Fisher equation by deriving local error bounds. In [19, 12], they have studied the local error estimates for the Strang splitting in time for the evolutionary Schrödinger equation and for the Schrödinger-Poisson equations, respectively. In [20], the local error bounds are constructed via the Strang splitting for partial differential equations with Burgers’ nonlinearity.

Operator splitting methods have also been investigated in fully discrete frameworks, where time splitting is combined with suitable spatial discretization techniques [23]. In [28, 29], operator splitting methods are coupled with finite difference spatial discretizations for reaction-diffusion systems, leading to fully discrete schemes that preserve the energetic variational structure and admit convergence analysis. In [27], a structure-preserving splitting scheme is proposed for reaction-diffusion equations with a detailed balance, where spatial discretization is based on finite differences while preserving key physical properties such as mass conservation and energy dissipation. For dispersive wave models, [30] develops a second-order accurate fully discrete scheme for the good Boussinesq equation by combining Strang splitting in time with a Fourier pseudo-spectral spatial discretization.In [22], an error analysis is presented for a fully discrete scheme for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, where Strang splitting is used for time integration and Hermite collocation for spatial discretization. In [24], a fully discrete error estimate is constructed with the Fourier collocation combined with the Strang splitting method for Benjamin-Bona-Mahony type equations. In [21], a Haar wavelet method integrated with the Strang splitting method is studied for the regularized long wave equation. A fully discrete scheme of a Strang splitting combined with Chebyshev wavelets is analyzed in [25]. In [26], an error estimate of a fully discrete spectral scheme is constructed for Boussinesq systems.

This work analyzes the Strang splitting combined with the Fourier collocation method for the fifth-order KBF equation (1) in the Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) Sobolev norm, assuming sufficient regularity of the exact solution and initial data

‖y⁡(t)‖Hs+11≤αand‖y0‖Hs+11≤β\|y(t)\|_{H^{s+11}}\leq\alpha\quad\mbox{and}\quad\|y_{0}\|_{H^{s+11}}\leq\beta (2)

for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T, where s,αs,\alpha and β\beta are given constants.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we analyze the convergence properties of the Strang splitting method for the fifth-order KdV–Burgers–Fisher equation, including regularity, stability, and error estimates in the Sobolev space HsH^{s}. In Section 3, we extend the analysis to the fully discrete scheme by combining the Strang splitting method with the Fourier collocation approach and derive the corresponding convergence results. Finally, in Section 4, we present a numerical experiment that confirms the theoretical findings.

2 Convergence Analysis of the Strang Splitting Method

In this section, we investigate the convergence properties of the Strang splitting method applied to the fifth-order KdV–Burgers–Fisher equation. The main objective is to establish error bounds in the Sobolev space HsH^{s}, under suitable regularity assumptions on the exact solution.

To construct the splitting scheme, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems corresponding to an unbounded linear operator and a bounded nonlinear operator. More precisely, we consider

ut=ν​∂x2u−μ​∂x3u+γ​∂x5u\displaystyle u_{t}=\nu\partial_{x}^{2}u-\mu\partial_{x}^{3}u+\gamma\partial_{x}^{5}u (3)

and

vt=−ε​v2​vx+ϵ​v​(1−v).\displaystyle v_{t}=-\varepsilon v^{2}v_{x}+\epsilon v(1-v). (4)

We now formulate the problem within the operator splitting framework. For the initial value problem

yt=E⁡(y),y⁡(t0)=y0,y_{t}=E(y),\quad y(t_{0})=y_{0},

we decompose the operator EE as E=A+BE=A+B. Let the solution of the initial value problem be represented by y⁡(t)=ΦEt​(y0)y(t)=\Phi^{t}_{E}(y_{0}). For n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\ldots and t=n​Δ​t≤Tt=n\Delta t\leq T, we define Strang splitting

yn+1=ΨΔ​t​(yn)=ΦAΔ​t/2∘ΦBΔ​t∘ΦAΔ​t/2​(yn),y_{n+1}=\Psi^{\Delta t}(y_{n})=\Phi^{\Delta t/2}_{A}\circ\Phi^{\Delta t}_{B}\circ\Phi^{\Delta t/2}_{A}(y_{n}), (5)

where

A​y=ν​∂x2y−μ​∂x3y+γ​∂x5yandB⁡(y)=−ε​y2​yx+ϵ​y​(1−y).Ay=\nu\partial_{x}^{2}y-\mu\partial_{x}^{3}y+\gamma\partial_{x}^{5}y\quad\mbox{and}\quad B(y)=-\varepsilon y^{2}y_{x}+\epsilon y(1-y).

The analysis proceeds by establishing regularity, stability, and error estimates for the Strang splitting method in HsH^{s}. The regularity requirement Hs+11H^{s+11} arises from the necessity to bound the double Lie commutators involving the fifth-order linear operator AA and the convective term in B⁡(u)B(u). Throughout the analysis, we use CC to denote a generic positive constant, not necessarily the same at each occurrence.

|∫ℝ∂xjv⋅∂xj(v2​vx)​𝑑x|≤C​‖v‖Hs4,|∫ℝ∂xjv⋅∂xj(v−v2)​𝑑x|≤C⁡(‖v‖Hs2+‖v‖Hs3).\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{x}^{j}v\cdot\partial_{x}^{j}(v^{2}v_{x})dx\right|\leq C\|v\|_{H^{s}}^{4},\quad\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_{x}^{j}v\cdot\partial_{x}^{j}(v-v^{2})dx\right|\leq C(\|v\|_{H^{s}}^{2}+\|v\|_{H^{s}}^{3}).

We proceed by deriving stability estimates in HsH^{s}.

Lemma 3

Let vv and v~\tilde{v} be two solutions of the nonlinear sub-problem (4) with initial data v0v_{0} associated with the splitting scheme. Assume that the solutions remain bounded in HsH^{s} such that ‖v⁡(t)‖Hs≤M\|v(t)\|_{H^{s}}\leq M and ‖v~​(t)‖Hs≤M\|\tilde{v}(t)\|_{H^{s}}\leq M for t∈[0,Δ​t]t\in[0,\Delta t]. Then, the following stability estimate holds:

‖v⁡(t)−v~​(t)‖Hs≤eL​t​‖v0−v~0‖Hs,\|v(t)-\tilde{v}(t)\|_{H^{s}}\leq\mathrm{e}^{Lt}\|v_{0}-\tilde{v}_{0}\|_{H^{s}}, (12)

where LL is a constant depending on ε,\varepsilon, ϵ\epsilon and MM.

Proof

The stability of the Strang splitting scheme is studied by examining the evolution of the difference between two numerical approximations. Since the linear operator A=ν∂x2−μ∂x3+γ∂x5A=\nu\partial_{x}^{2}-\mu\partial_{x}^{3}+\gamma\partial_{x}^{5} generates a flow ΦAt\Phi_{A}^{t} that is preserved in the HsH^{s} norm, the stability of the full splitting step is determined primarily by the nonlinear flow ΦBt\Phi_{B}^{t}. Let vv and v~\tilde{v} be two solutions satisfying the nonlinear sub-problem vt=B⁡(v)v_{t}=B(v) and v~t=B⁡(v~)\tilde{v}_{t}=B(\tilde{v}), where the operator is defined as B⁡(v)=−ε​v2​vx+ϵ​v−ϵ​v2B(v)=-\varepsilon v^{2}v_{x}+\epsilon v-\epsilon v^{2}. The difference v−v~v-\tilde{v} satisfies the equation (v−v~)t=B⁡(v)−B⁡(v~)(v-\tilde{v})_{t}=B(v)-B(\tilde{v}), and by taking the HsH^{s} norm, we obtain the integral inequality

‖v⁡(t)−v~​(t)‖Hs≤‖v0−v~0‖Hs+∫0t‖B⁡(v⁡(τ))−B⁡(v~​(τ))‖Hs​𝑑τ.\|v(t)-\tilde{v}(t)\|_{H^{s}}\leq\|v_{0}-\tilde{v}_{0}\|_{H^{s}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|B(v(\tau))-B(\tilde{v}(\tau))\|_{H^{s}}d\tau.

To derive the Lipschitz constant LL, we estimate the difference B⁡(v)−B⁡(v~)B(v)-B(\tilde{v}) using standard product bounds in the Sobolev space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}). The linear component ϵ⁡(v−v~)\epsilon(v-\tilde{v}) yields a direct bound proportional to ϵ​‖v−v~‖Hs\epsilon\|v-\tilde{v}\|_{H^{s}}. For the quadratic part ϵ⁡(v2−v~2)\epsilon(v^{2}-\tilde{v}^{2}), the algebraic property leads to a bound involving ‖v‖Hs​‖v−v~‖Hs\|v\|_{H^{s}}\|v-\tilde{v}\|_{H^{s}}. The most complex term, the cubic nonlinearity with a spatial derivative −ε⁡(v2​vx−v~2​v~x)-\varepsilon(v^{2}v_{x}-\tilde{v}^{2}\tilde{v}_{x}), is decomposed as −ε⁡[v2​(vx−v~x)+(v2−v~2)​v~x]-\varepsilon[v^{2}(v_{x}-\tilde{v}_{x})+(v^{2}-\tilde{v}^{2})\tilde{v}_{x}]. Applying Sobolev inequalities and the boundedness of the flow from Lemma 1, this term is bounded by C⁡(‖v‖Hs2+‖v~‖Hs2)​‖v−v~‖HsC(\|v\|_{H^{s}}^{2}+\|\tilde{v}\|_{H^{s}}^{2})\|v-\tilde{v}\|_{H^{s}}. Summing these individual estimates, we arrive at the Lipschitz bound ‖B⁡(v)−B⁡(v~)‖Hs≤(ϵ+C1​‖v‖Hs+C2​‖v‖Hs2)​‖v−v~‖Hs\|B(v)-B(\tilde{v})\|_{H^{s}}\leq(\epsilon+C_{1}\|v\|_{H^{s}}+C_{2}\|v\|_{H^{s}}^{2})\|v-\tilde{v}\|_{H^{s}}. By defining LL as a constant that incorporates the linear coefficient ϵ\epsilon and the higher-order norms required by the cubic term, we apply Gronwall’s lemma to conclude the stability of the nonlinear flow. Since the linear flows ΦAΔ​t/2\Phi_{A}^{\Delta t/2} in the Strang sequence do not increase the HsH^{s} norm, the stability of the full step is preserved.

2.3 Local Error

We establish a local error bound for the Strang splitting scheme.

Lemma 4

If the initial data y0y_{0} is in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), then the local error of the Strang splitting (5) is

‖ΨΔ​t​(y0)−ΦΔ​t​(y0)‖Hs≤C​Δ​t3,\|\Psi^{\Delta t}(y_{0})-\Phi^{\Delta t}(y_{0})\|_{H^{s}}\leq C\Delta t^{3}, (13)

Substituting this expansion into Equation (14) yields the Strang splitting approximation

2.4 Global error in HsH^{s} space

We obtain a global error bound by combining the stability and the local error bounds.

Theorem 2.1

Suppose that the exact solution y⁡(⋅,t)y(\cdot,t) of Equation (1) is in HsH^{s} for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T. Then the Strang splitting solution yny_{n} given in Equation (5) has second-order global error for Δ​t<Δ​t¯\Delta t<\bar{\Delta t} and tn=n​Δ​t≤Tt_{n}=n\Delta t\leq T,

‖yn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs≤G​Δ​t2,\displaystyle\|y_{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}}\leq G{\Delta t}^{2},

where GG only depends on ‖y0‖Hs\|y_{0}\|_{H^{s}}, α\alpha and T.T.

Proof

In the proof we employ the Lady Windermere’s fan argument to derive the global error bound from the local consistency and stability properties. The required stability estimate and local error bound are provided in Lemma 3 and Lemma 4, respectively. Let

y⁡(tn)=Φ(n−k)​Δ​t​(y⁡(tk))y(t_{n})=\Phi^{(n-k)\Delta t}(y(t_{k}))

denote the exact solution of Equation (1) at time tnt_{n}, starting from the value y⁡(tk)y(t_{k}) at time tkt_{k}. The numerical approximation generated by the Strang splitting scheme satisfies the recurrence relation

yn=ΨΔ​t(yn−1)=ΦAΔ​t/2∘ΦBΔ​t∘ΦAΔ​t/2(yn−1),n=1,2,….y_{n}=\Psi^{\Delta t}(y_{n-1})=\Phi^{\Delta t/2}_{A}\circ\Phi^{\Delta t}_{B}\circ\Phi^{\Delta t/2}_{A}(y_{n-1}),\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.

We compare the numerical flow with the exact evolution and estimate the error in the HsH^{s} norm. By a telescopic expansion of the global error, we obtain

‖yn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs\displaystyle\|y_{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}} ≤∑k=0n−1‖Ψ(n−k−1)​Δ​t​(ΦΔ​t​(y⁡(tk))−ΨΔ​t​(y⁡(tk)))‖Hs\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\|\Psi^{(n-k-1)\Delta t}(\Phi^{\Delta t}(y(t_{k}))-\Psi^{\Delta t}(y(t_{k})))\|_{H^{s}}
≤∑k=0n−1eL⁡(n−k−1)​Δ​t​‖ΦΔ​t​(y⁡(tk))−ΨΔ​t​(y⁡(tk))‖Hs.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathrm{e}^{L(n-k-1)\Delta t}\|\Phi^{\Delta t}(y(t_{k}))-\Psi^{\Delta t}(y(t_{k}))\|_{H^{s}}.

Using the stability bound together with the local error estimate, and noting that n​Δ​t≤Tn\Delta t\leq T, we arrive at

‖yn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs\displaystyle\|y_{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}} ≤∑k=0n−1eL​T​C​Δ​t3\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathrm{e}^{LT}C\Delta t^{3}
≤n​eL​T​C​Δ​t3\displaystyle\leq n\mathrm{e}^{LT}C\Delta t^{3}
≤T​eL​T​C​Δ​t2.\displaystyle\leq T\mathrm{e}^{LT}C\Delta t^{2}.

This establishes the second-order convergence in time.

3 Convergence Analysis of the Strang Splitting Combined with the Fourier Collocation Method

In this section, we begin by deriving a semi-discrete scheme and then proceed to construct a fully discrete scheme. Afterwards, the convergence of the fully discrete scheme is investigated in a step-by-step manner.

3.1 Semi-discrete collocation scheme of the Fifth-Order KdV-Burgers-Fisher Equation

In this section, the solution y⁡(x,t)y(x,t) corresponding to Equation (1) is approximated by trigonometric basis functions for every fixed tt, as given below:

y(x,t)≃yN(x,t)=∑k=−N/2N/2−1y^k(t)ei​k​x,\displaystyle y(x,t)\simeq y_{N}(x,t)=\sum_{k=-N/2}^{N/2-1}\hat{y}_{k}(t)e^{ikx}, (22)

where −π≤x≤π,-\pi\leq x\leq\pi, N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, y^k​(t)\hat{y}_{k}(t) represents the unknown Fourier coefficients, which are computed using the Fourier collocation method presented in [23, 31]. Let BN={ei​k​x:−N/2≤k≤N/2−1}B_{N}=\{e^{ikx}:-N/2\leq k\leq N/2-1\} be the function space. Fourier interpolation operator, IN:C⁡(−π,π)→BN,I_{N}:C(-\pi,\pi)\rightarrow B_{N}, is expressed by

INy(xl)=y(xl),l=−N/2,⋯,N/2−1,\displaystyle I_{N}y(x_{l})=y(x_{l}),\,\ l=-N/2,\cdots,N/2-1, (23)

where xl=2​π​lN,l=−N/2,⋯,N/2−1x_{l}=\frac{2\pi l}{N},\,\ l=-N/2,\cdots,N/2-1 are any collocation points. A Fourier-interpolated function y⁡(x)y(x) can be represented as follows:

INy(x)=∑k=−N/2N/2−1y^kei​k​x,\displaystyle I_{N}y(x)=\sum_{k=-N/2}^{N/2-1}\hat{y}_{k}e^{ikx}, (24)

where {y^k}k=−N/2N/2−1=ℱ(y(xl))l=−N/2N/2−1\{\hat{y}_{k}\}_{k=-N/2}^{N/2-1}=\mathcal{F}(y(x_{l}))_{l=-N/2}^{N/2-1} and ℱ\mathcal{F} is discrete Fourier transform.

The semi-discrete Fourier collocation algorithm for Equation (1) is

yN,t​(xl,t)\displaystyle y_{N,t}(x_{l},t) =ν​yN,x​x​(xl,t)−μ​yN,x​x​x​(xl,t)+γ​yN,x​x​x​x​x​(xl,t)\displaystyle=\nu y_{N,xx}(x_{l},t)-\mu y_{N,xxx}(x_{l},t)+\gamma y_{N,xxxxx}(x_{l},t)
−ε​IN​(yN2​(xl,t)​yN,x​(xl,t))+ϵ​IN​(yN​(xl,t)​(1−yN​(xl,t))),\displaystyle-\varepsilon I_{N}\bigl(y_{N}^{2}(x_{l},t)\,y_{N,x}(x_{l},t)\bigr)+\epsilon I_{N}\bigl(y_{N}(x_{l},t)\bigl(1-y_{N}(x_{l},t)\bigr)\bigr),
yN​(xl,0)\displaystyle y_{N}(x_{l},0) =IN​y0​(xl).\displaystyle=I_{N}y_{0}(x_{l}). (25)

where yN​(xl,t)∈BN,y_{N}(x_{l},t)\in B_{N}, for −N2≤l≤N2−1-\frac{N}{2}\leq l\leq\frac{N}{2}-1 .

3.2 A fully discrete collocation scheme for the fifth-order KdV-Burgers-Fisher equation

In this section, a fully discrete approximation of Equation (1) is developed by employing the Strang splitting technique for the temporal discretization and a Fourier collocation approach for the spatial variables. Hence, the semi-discrete Equation (25) is split into linear and nonlinear parts as follows:

yN,t\displaystyle y_{N,t} =ν​yN,x​x−μ​yN,x​x​x+γ​yN,x​x​x​x​x,\displaystyle=\nu y_{N,xx}-\mu y_{N,xxx}+\gamma y_{N,xxxxx}, (26)
yN,t\displaystyle y_{N,t} =−ε​IN​(yN2​yN,x)+ϵ​IN​(yN​(1−yN)).\displaystyle=-\varepsilon I_{N}\bigl(y_{N}^{2}\,y_{N,x}\bigr)+\epsilon I_{N}\bigl(y_{N}\bigl(1-y_{N}\bigr)\bigr).\ \ (27)

Let us assume that the fully discrete solution is yNny_{N}^{n} at time tn=n​Δ​tt_{n}=n\Delta t with time step Δ​t\Delta t, ΩNΔ​t\Omega_{N}^{\Delta t} is the full propagator, ΩB​NΔ​t\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t} is the full discrete propagator for the nonlinear part after one time step of Δ​t,\Delta t, and yN0=IN​(y⁡(⋅,0))y_{N}^{0}=I_{N}(y(\cdot,0)). Hence, the fully discrete scheme is as follows

yNn+1=ΩNΔ​t​(yNn)=eΔt(ν∂2x−μ∂3x+γ∂5x)2​ΩB​NΔ​t​eΔt(ν∂2x−μ∂3x+γ∂5x)2​yNn.\displaystyle y_{N}^{n+1}=\Omega_{N}^{\Delta t}(y_{N}^{n})=e^{\frac{{\Delta t(\nu\partial^{2}_{x}-\mu\partial^{3}_{x}+\gamma\partial^{5}_{x}})}{2}}\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t}e^{\frac{{\Delta t(\nu\partial^{2}_{x}-\mu\partial^{3}_{x}+\gamma\partial^{5}_{x}})}{2}}y_{N}^{n}. (28)

Here, the exponential method is utilized for the solution of the linear part while any suitable approximate method can be utilized for nonlinear part.

3.3 Convergence Analysis of the Fully-discrete Scheme

In this section, we first introduce the Fourier interpolation lemmas. Then we develop stability, consistency and convergence error bounds for the fully discrete algorithm (28).

Let yNny_{N}^{n} be the fully discrete solution and y⁡(⋅,tn)y(\cdot,t_{n}) be the analytical solution at time tn=n​Δ​tt_{n}=n\Delta t of Equation (1). In order to study the fully discrete error, we start with the following error bound

‖yNn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs≤‖yNn−yn‖Hs+‖yn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs,\displaystyle\|y_{N}^{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}}\leq\|y_{N}^{n}-y_{n}\|_{H^{s}}+\|y_{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}}, (29)

where yny_{n} is the time-discrete solution given in Section 2. The second term on the right-hand side of inequality (29) is the time-discrete global error bound given in Theorem 2.1. The first term on the right-hand side of inequality (29) can be written as follows

‖yNn−yn‖Hs≤‖yNn−IN​yn‖Hs+‖IN​yn−yn‖Hs,\displaystyle\|y_{N}^{n}-y_{n}\|_{H^{s}}\leq\|y_{N}^{n}-I_{N}y_{n}\|_{H^{s}}+\|I_{N}y_{n}-y_{n}\|_{H^{s}}, (30)

where INI_{N} is the Fourier interpolation operator.

Here, lemmas related to the Fourier interpolation operator are presented.

Lemma 5

Let yy be a 2​π2\pi periodic function such that ∂xmy∈L2,\partial^{m}_{x}y\in L^{2}, for some m≥1.m\geq 1. Then the interpolation error is bounded in L2L^{2} by

‖y−IN​y‖L2≤G​N−m​‖∂xmy‖L2,\displaystyle\|y-I_{N}y\|_{L^{2}}\leq GN^{-m}\|\partial^{m}_{x}y\|_{L^{2}}, (31)

where GG depends only on mm. And for any integer d≥1d\geq 1,

‖∂xd(y−IN​y)‖L2≤G​N−m​‖∂xm+dy‖L2.\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}^{d}(y-I_{N}y)\|_{L^{2}}\leq GN^{-m}\|\partial^{m+d}_{x}y\|_{L^{2}}. (32)
Proof

See [23, Theorem 1.7].

Lemma 6

Let yy be a 2​π2\pi periodic function such that ∂xmy∈Hs,\partial^{m}_{x}y\in H^{s}, for some m≥1.m\geq 1. Then the interpolation error is bounded in HsH^{s} by

‖y−IN​y‖Hs≤G​N−m​‖y‖Hm+s,\displaystyle\|y-I_{N}y\|_{H^{s}}\leq GN^{-m}\|y\|_{H^{m+s}}, (33)

where GG depends only on mm. And for any integer d≥1,d\geq 1,

‖∂xd(y−IN​y)‖Hs≤G​N−m​‖y‖Hm+s+d.\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}^{d}(y-I_{N}y)\|_{H^{s}}\leq GN^{-m}\|y\|_{H^{m+s+d}}. (34)
Proof

See [24, Lemma 2.1].

Lemma 7 (Stability of Fourier interpolation)

Let yy and vv be 2​π2\pi periodic functions such that y,v∈Hsy,v\in H^{s}, with s>0.s>0. Then the Fourier interpolation operator satisfies the following

‖IN​(y)‖Hs\displaystyle\left\|I_{N}(y)\right\|_{H^{s}} ≤K0​‖y‖Hs,\displaystyle\leq K_{0}\left\|y\right\|_{H^{s}}, (35)
‖IN​(y​v)‖Hs\displaystyle\left\|I_{N}(yv)\right\|_{H^{s}} ≤K1​‖IN​y‖Hs​‖IN​v‖Hs,\displaystyle\leq K_{1}\left\|I_{N}y\right\|_{H^{s}}\left\|I_{N}v\right\|_{H^{s}},\ \ (36)

where K0K_{0} and K1K_{1} are independent of N.N.

Proof

Using the boundedness of the Fourier interpolation operator in HsH^{s} together with the algebra property of HsH^{s} for s>0s>0, we obtain inequalities (35) and (36), see [23, 31].

Lemma 8

Let y,v∈Hs​(−π,π)y,v\in H^{s}(-\pi,\pi). Then there exists a constant G>0G>0 such that

‖∂xIN​(y​v)‖Hs≤G​‖IN​y‖Hs​‖IN​v‖Hs.\|\partial_{x}I_{N}(yv)\|_{H^{s}}\leq G\,\|I_{N}y\|_{H^{s}}\,\|I_{N}v\|_{H^{s}}. (37)
Proof

We recall that the Fourier interpolation of the product y​vyv can be written as

IN​(y​v)​(x)=∑k=−N2N2−1hk​ei​k​x,I_{N}(yv)(x)=\sum_{k=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}h_{k}e^{ikx},

where hk=ℱ⁡(y⁡(xj)​v​(xj))=∑ℓ=−N2N2−1y^k−ℓ​v^ℓ,h_{k}=\mathcal{F}\big(y(x_{j})v(x_{j})\big)=\sum_{\ell=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}\hat{y}_{k-\ell}\,\hat{v}_{\ell}, −N2≤j≤N2.-\frac{N}{2}\leq j\leq\frac{N}{2}. Starting from the left-hand side of (37), we have

‖∂xIN​(y​v)‖Hs≤∑j=0s‖∂xj+1IN​(y​v)‖L2.\|\partial_{x}I_{N}(yv)\|_{H^{s}}\leq\sum_{j=0}^{s}\|\partial_{x}^{\,j+1}I_{N}(yv)\|_{L^{2}}.

We first consider the highest-order term:

‖∂xs+1IN​(y​v)‖L22\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}^{\,s+1}I_{N}(yv)\|_{L^{2}}^{2} =‖∂xs+1(∑k=−N2N2−1hk​ei​k​x)‖L22\displaystyle=\left\|\partial_{x}^{\,s+1}\left(\sum_{k=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}h_{k}e^{ikx}\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

≤G​(∑ℓ=−N2N2−1|(k−ℓ)s​y^k−ℓ|2)1/2​(∑ℓ=−N2N2−1|ℓs​v^ℓ|2)1/2,\displaystyle\leq G\left(\sum_{\ell=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}|(k-\ell)^{s}\hat{y}_{k-\ell}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{\ell=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}|\ell^{s}\hat{v}_{\ell}|^{2}\right)^{1/2},\ \

where the constants maxk,ℓ⁡|ks(k−ℓ)s​ℓs|\max_{k,\ell}\left|\frac{k^{s}}{(k-\ell)^{s}\,\ell^{s}}\right| and ∑k=−N2N2−1|k|2\sum_{k=-\frac{N}{2}}^{\frac{N}{2}-1}|k|^{2} are bounded by positive constants G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, respectively, and G=G1⋅G2.G=G_{1}\cdot G_{2}. Hence,

‖∂xs+1IN​(y​v)‖L2≤G​‖IN​y‖Hs​‖IN​v‖Hs.\|\partial_{x}^{\,s+1}I_{N}(yv)\|_{L^{2}}\leq G\,\|I_{N}y\|_{H^{s}}\,\|I_{N}v\|_{H^{s}}.

The lower-order terms can be treated similarly, which completes the proof.

Lemma 10 (Stability)

Let y0,y~0∈Hsy_{0},\widetilde{y}_{0}\in H^{s}. Then

‖ΩNΔ​t​(y0)−ΩNΔ​t​(y~0)‖Hs\displaystyle\left\|\Omega_{N}^{\Delta t}(y_{0})-\Omega_{N}^{\Delta t}(\widetilde{y}_{0})\right\|_{H^{s}} ≤eKs​Δ​t​‖y0−y~0‖Hs,\displaystyle\leq e^{K_{s}\Delta t}\left\|y_{0}-\widetilde{y}_{0}\right\|_{H^{s}},\ \ (43)

where Ks=K1​K02​ε​(Ms2+1+Ms)K_{s}=K_{1}K^{2}_{0}\,\varepsilon(M^{2}_{s}+1+M_{s}) with sup0≤t≤Δ​t(‖ΩB​NΔ​t​(y0)‖Hs+‖ΩB​NΔ​t​(y~0)‖Hs)≤Ms\sup_{0\leq t\leq\Delta t}(\|\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t}(y_{0})\|_{H^{s}}+\|\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t}(\widetilde{y}_{0})\|_{H^{s}})\leq M_{s}.

Proof

We know that linear operator eΔt(ν∂2x−μ∂3x+γ∂5x)2e^{\frac{{\Delta t(\nu\partial^{2}_{x}-\mu\partial^{3}_{x}+\gamma\partial^{5}_{x}})}{2}} is preserved in the HsH^{s} norm. Hence it is sufficient to bound the nonlinear part. Let ΩB​NΔ​t​(y0)=Λ⁡(Δ​t)\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t}(y_{0})=\Lambda(\Delta t) and ΩB​NΔ​t​(y~0)=Γ⁡(Δ​t),\Omega_{BN}^{\Delta t}(\widetilde{y}_{0})=\Gamma(\Delta t), where Δ​t\Delta t is the time step. Consider the following equations satisfying the nonlinear part:

∂tΛ\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Lambda =−ε​IN​(Λ2​∂xΛ)+ϵ​IN​(Λ⁡(1−Λ)),Λ⁡(0)=y0,\displaystyle=-\varepsilon\,I_{N}\!\left(\Lambda^{2}\,\partial_{x}\Lambda\right)+\epsilon\,I_{N}\!\left(\Lambda(1-\Lambda)\right),\qquad\Lambda(0)=y_{0}, (44)

≤0,\displaystyle\leq 0, (54)

since R​e​(−ν​ξ2+μ⁡(i​ξ3)+γ⁡(i​ξ5))≤0Re(-\nu\xi^{2}+\mu(i\xi^{3})+\gamma(i\xi^{5}))\leq 0 with ν>0.\nu>0. Therefore, the first term of Equation (53) is neglected. Applying Lemma 6 to the second term on the right-hand side of (53) yields the following expression

In order to obtain the global error bound of the fully discretized scheme, Lady Windermere’s fan argument, which combines the local error bound given in Lemma 11 with stability result given in Lemma 10, will be used. In what follows, we assume that

‖yNn−IN​(yn)‖Hs\displaystyle\|y_{N}^{n}-I_{N}(y_{n})\|_{H^{s}} ≤P​N−m​(eH​ρ3​(n)​n​Δ​t−1H​ρ3​(n)),\displaystyle\leq PN^{-m}\left(\frac{e^{H\rho_{3}(n)n\Delta t}-1}{H\rho_{3}(n)}\right), (61)

where PP depends on m,m, s,s, T,T, sup0≤t≤T‖y⁡(⋅,τ)‖Hm+s+5.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|y(\cdot,\tau)\|_{H^{m+s+5}}. Then rearranging (61) with the help of the Lemma 6 yields

Hence, suppose that ρ3​(n)≤2​P\rho_{3}(n)\leq 2P where PP is given in (62) with n​Δ​t≤Tn\Delta t\leq T for large N.N. The inequality (62) is satisfied for ‖(ΩNΔ​t)n−j​(IN​(yj))−yn‖Hs\|(\Omega_{N}^{\Delta t})^{n-j}(I_{N}(y_{j}))-y_{n}\|_{H^{s}} with j=0,⋯,n.j=0,\cdots,n. Then for each jj we get

Theorem 3.1 (Global error)

Let the exact solution of the fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers-Fisher equation (1), y=y⁡(x,t),y=y(x,t), be in Hm+s+5H^{m+s+5} for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and x∈[−π,π]x\in[-\pi,\pi]. Then the fully discrete solution (28) has the following error bound

‖yNn−y⁡(⋅,tn)‖Hs≤P⁡(N−m+Δ​t2),\displaystyle\|y_{N}^{n}-y(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{H^{s}}\leq P(N^{-m}+\Delta t^{2}), (65)

where tn=n​Δ​t,t_{n}=n\Delta t, PP depends on m, s, T and My=max0≤t≤T⁡‖y⁡(⋅,t)‖Hm+s+5.M_{y}=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\|y(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{m+s+5}}.

4 Numerical Results

For the numerical confirmation of the convergence results, Equation (1) is split into two sub-equations

yt​(x,t)\displaystyle y_{t}(x,t) =ν​yx​x​(x,t)−μ​yx​x​x​(x,t)+γ​yx​x​x​x​x​(x,t),\displaystyle=\nu y_{xx}(x,t)-\mu y_{xxx}(x,t)+\gamma y_{xxxxx}(x,t), (66)
yt​(x,t)\displaystyle y_{t}(x,t) =−ε​y2​(x,t)​yx​(x,t)+ϵ​y​(x,t)​(1−y⁡(x,t)),\displaystyle=-\varepsilon y^{2}(x,t)y_{x}(x,t)+\epsilon y(x,t)\bigl(1-y(x,t)\bigr), (67)

which are then solved successively.

We apply the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) to discretize the subproblems (66) and (67) in the spatial variable. Consider Equation (66) in the interval x∈[0,2​π]x\in[0,2\pi] for t>0t>0 together with periodic boundary conditions. In this case, the solution y⁡(x,t)y(x,t) can be represented by the Fourier series [31]

y⁡(x,t)=∑k=−∞∞y^k​(t)​ei​k​x,\displaystyle y(x,t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\hat{y}_{k}(t)e^{ikx}, (68)

where y^k\hat{y}_{k} denotes the Fourier coefficients corresponding to the initial data.

On a uniform grid with spacing h=2​πNh=\frac{2\pi}{N}, the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is defined as

y^k(t)=h∑j=1Nyj(t)e−i​k​xj,k=−N2+1,…,N2,\displaystyle\hat{y}_{k}(t)=h\sum_{j=1}^{N}y_{j}(t)e^{-ikx_{j}},\qquad k=-\frac{N}{2}+1,\ldots,\frac{N}{2}, (69)

while the inverse discrete Fourier transform (IDFT) is given by [31]

yj(t)=12​π∑k=−N/2+1N/2y^k(t)ei​k​xj,j=1,…,N.\displaystyle y_{j}(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{k=-N/2+1}^{N/2}\hat{y}_{k}(t)e^{ikx_{j}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,N. (70)

We employ the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for computation of the DFT [31]. Applying the DFT to Equation (66) yields

dd​t​y^k​(t)=(−ν​k2+i​μ​k3−i​γ​k5)​y^k​(t),y^k​(0)=y^0​k,\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\hat{y}_{k}(t)=(-\nu k^{2}+i\mu k^{3}-i\gamma k^{5})\hat{y}_{k}(t),\qquad\hat{y}_{k}(0)=\hat{y}_{0k}, (71)

and the solution is given as

y^k(t)=e(−ν​k2+i​μ​k3−i​γ​k5)​ty^0​k,k=−N/2+1,…,N/2.\hat{y}_{k}(t)=e^{(-\nu k^{2}+i\mu k^{3}-i\gamma k^{5})t}\hat{y}_{0k},\qquad k=-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2.

We now apply the DFT to Equation (67) and then we have

dd​t​y^k​(t)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\hat{y}_{k}(t) =−ε3​i​k​ℱ​((ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))3)\displaystyle=-\frac{\varepsilon}{3}ik\,\mathcal{F}\Bigl((\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t)))^{3}\Bigr)
+ϵ​ℱ​(ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))\displaystyle\quad+\epsilon\,\mathcal{F}\Bigl(\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t))\Bigr)
−ϵ​ℱ​((ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))2).\displaystyle\quad-\epsilon\,\mathcal{F}\Bigl((\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t)))^{2}\Bigr). (72)

Equation (72) can also be written as

dd​t​Y=F⁡(Y),\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}Y=F(Y), (73)

where k=−N/2+1,…,N/2k=-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2, y^k​(t)=Y\hat{y}_{k}(t)=Y, F⁡(Y)=−ε3​i​k​ℱ​((ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))3)+ϵ​ℱ​(ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))−ϵ​ℱ​((ℱ−1​(y^k​(t)))2).F(Y)=-\frac{\varepsilon}{3}ik\,\mathcal{F}\!\left((\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t)))^{3}\right)+\epsilon\mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t))\right)-\epsilon\mathcal{F}\!\left((\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{y}_{k}(t)))^{2}\right). We approximate Equation (73) with the fourth order Runge-Kutta method as follows

a\displaystyle a =\displaystyle= F⁡(Yn)\displaystyle F(Y_{n})
b\displaystyle b =\displaystyle= F⁡(Yn+Δ​t2​k1)\displaystyle F(Y_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{1})
c\displaystyle c =\displaystyle= F⁡(Yn+Δ​t2​k2)\displaystyle F(Y_{n}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{2})
d\displaystyle d =\displaystyle= F⁡(Yn+Δ​t​k3)\displaystyle F(Y_{n}+\Delta tk_{3})
Yn+1\displaystyle Y_{n+1} =\displaystyle= Yn+16​Δ​t​(a+2​b+2​c+d)\displaystyle Y_{n}+\frac{1}{6}\Delta t(a+2b+2c+d) (74)

where Δ​t\Delta t is the time step. On the other hand, in order to obtain reference solutions numerically, we employ the method of integrating factors with the classical fourth order Runge-Kutta method applied to Equation (1).

Example

Let us examine Equation (1) with the initial condition defined as

y⁡(x,0)=12+14​sin⁡(x),y(x,0)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\sin(x), (75)

under the assumption of periodic boundary conditions in the space domain [0,2​π][0,2\pi]. The parameters are chosen as ν=1\nu=1, μ=1.0\mu=1.0, ε=1\varepsilon=1, ϵ=1\epsilon=1, and γ=1.0\gamma=1.0. We perform the spatial discretization using N=256N=256 collocation points. The error at the final time is measured using the 2-norm error. In Fig. 1, we show the performance of the Strang splitting method by plotting the solution error versus the number of steps. The observed convergence orders are presented in Table 1. The lines in Fig. 1 and the values reported in Table 1 verify the theoretical results of second-order convergence.

5 Conclusion

A numerical approximation scheme has been constructed efficiently by combining the Fourier collocation method in spatial discretization with the Strang splitting technique in time integration for the fifth-order Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers-Fisher equation (KBF). In the first part of the paper, the convergence of the time discrete scheme, which is constructed by Strang splitting, has been proved with the help of numerical quadratures using Lie commutator bounds under suitable regularity assumptions. Then, the convergence of the full discrete scheme has been successfully established by analyzing the global time discretization error and the Fourier interpolation error. Finally, the computational findings demonstrate that the proposed scheme ensures spatial accuracy together with second order temporal accuracy.
